The Case for [APP NAME]

24

Anish Velagapudi • Kenan Snider • Baylee Varnell • Gina Byon

Statement of the Problem

32

33 Misinformation today rarely takes the form of outright lies — it hides in the 34 architecture of how information is presented. A bar graph with a manipulated 35 baseline, a headline missing critical context, or a statistic cited without its 36 denominator can shape public opinion just as powerfully as fabricated news, yet 37 none of these techniques constitute a factual falsehood that traditional 38 fact-checkers are designed to catch. 39

40

41 According to a 2024 Gallup poll, 42 only 32% of Americans have a "great deal" or "fair amount" of trust in mass media. 43 This erosion of trust suggests that the public senses manipulation but lacks the 44 tools to identify it precisely. The result is a lose-lose: people are either 45 deceived by misleading framing they cannot detect, or they dismiss all media as 46 untrustworthy — an overcorrection that accelerates polarization and makes 47 evidence-based public discourse nearly impossible. 48

49

50 [APP NAME] addresses this gap by giving ordinary users the same analytical tools 51 that trained media critics use — automatically, in real time, and without 52 requiring expertise. This invention is important because the capacity to recognize 53 manipulation is not evenly distributed, and that inequality in media literacy has 54 measurable consequences for how people vote, how they respond to public health 55 guidance, and how they understand their world. 56

57 58 59

Supporting Research

60
Finding 1
61

62 Online misinformation and deceptive presentation are widespread and growing problems 63

64

65 A comprehensive survey by 66 Security.org (2024) 67 found that the vast majority of Americans report regularly encountering misinformation 68 online, and a significant portion report being unable to identify it when they do. 69 Crucially, the study distinguishes between outright disinformation (deliberately false 70 content) and misinformation — inaccurate or misleading content spread regardless of 71 intent. Misleading presentation of true facts falls squarely in the latter 72 category and is far more common, precisely because it is harder to challenge. 73

74

75 Deceptive data visualizations are a particularly under-studied vector. Research in 76 data journalism and information design has catalogued dozens of chart manipulation 77 techniques — from truncated y-axes to dual-axis graphs that imply false correlations — 78 that routinely appear in mainstream media without any correction or notice. 79 [APP NAME]'s chart analysis module specifically targets this gap. 80

81 82 83
Finding 2
84

85 The market for AI-powered media literacy tools is large, underserved, and commercially viable 86

87

88 According to 89 Statista, 90 there are approximately 331 million internet users in the United States in 2026. 91 Even capturing 1% of that audience as active users — a conservative benchmark for 92 a niche tool — produces a user base of 3.3 million people. At a modest $1 per user 93 per year in ad revenue (industry standard for content-adjacent apps), that floor 94 generates over $3 million annually without a single paid subscriber. 95

96

97 The revenue ceiling is substantially higher. Data from 98 ReachEffect 99 shows that subscription app users generate on average 4.6 times the revenue of 100 ad-only users. A premium tier priced at $5/month — positioned as a civic tool 101 comparable to a news subscription — could push annual revenue to $13–14 million 102 if just 10–15% of active users convert. No direct competitor in the real-time 103 manipulation-detection space currently exists at consumer scale, meaning [APP NAME] 104 has an opportunity to define the category. 105

106 107

Brief Description of the Invention

108

109 [APP NAME] is a browser extension and mobile application that uses artificial 110 intelligence to analyze news articles, data visualizations, and video content in 111 real time, flagging patterns of misrepresentation and categorizing them by type. 112 Unlike conventional fact-checkers, which verify factual claims against databases 113 of known falsehoods, [APP NAME] evaluates the structural integrity of how 114 information is presented — detecting manipulated chart baselines, decontextualized 115 statistics, emotionally loaded framing paired with thin evidence, and missing 116 comparative data. 117

118

119 Key features include: real-time scanning with no user input required; a 120 categorized flag system that explains how and why content may be 121 misleading; a chart integrity module using computer vision; video transcript 122 analysis; and a free tier with an optional premium subscription. The system is 123 designed to be privacy-preserving, performing analysis on-device where possible 124 and never storing identifiable browsing data. 125

126 127

Policy Implications

128

129 Policymakers should recognize AI-powered media literacy tools as a complement — 130 not a replacement — for platform-level content moderation. Regulatory frameworks 131 should encourage transparency in AI flagging methodologies and mandate bias audits 132 for tools operating at scale. [APP NAME] demonstrates that the market can produce 133 consumer-grade media literacy technology, but government investment in public 134 education programs and potential subsidies for underserved communities could 135 dramatically expand access. Key regulatory challenges include defining "misleading 136 presentation" in a legally coherent way, avoiding chilling effects on legitimate 137 journalism, and ensuring algorithmic accountability. 138

Ethics & Privacy

Built Responsibly

An app designed to fight manipulation must be held to a higher standard of transparency. Here's how we think about the hard questions.

Ethical Challenges

The hard questions we ask ourselves

⚖️ Who decides what counts as "misleading"?

Defining misrepresentation is itself a subjective act. [APP NAME] mitigates this by focusing on structural manipulation patterns — e.g., a bar chart with a truncated y-axis — rather than making political or factual truth judgments. Our taxonomy of manipulation types is publicly documented and open to community feedback, and we plan to work with media literacy researchers to refine it over time.

🤖 Algorithmic Bias

AI models reflect the data they are trained on. If our training data overrepresents certain media outlets, political viewpoints, or languages, the model will be systematically biased in its flags. We address this through diverse training corpora, regular bias audits, and making our flagging methodology transparent. Users can always see why content was flagged — not just that it was.

🗣️ Chilling Effects on Speech

A tool that flags content as misleading could discourage creators from publishing nuanced or unconventional analysis — even when that analysis is legitimate. We are careful to frame flags as "potential concerns" rather than verdicts, and we always include an explanation. Publishers whose content is flagged can submit a formal review request.

🔁 Creating New Misinformation

If users blindly trust [APP NAME]'s outputs, we risk replacing one form of misinformation dependency with another. Our Explanation Mode is designed to build the user's own critical thinking skills — not to be an oracle. We prominently display confidence levels and encourage independent verification.

📡 Surveillance Risk

Scanning content you browse creates a detailed picture of your media consumption. [APP NAME] uses on-device processing wherever possible and never stores browsing history on our servers without explicit consent. We will never sell data to advertisers, data brokers, or government agencies.

Mitigation

How we address these concerns

📖

Open Methodology

Our taxonomy of manipulation patterns is publicly available. Anyone can read, critique, and propose changes to how we define misrepresentation.

🧪

Regular Bias Audits

Third-party researchers will conduct periodic audits of the model's outputs across political spectrum, geography, and language.

🙋

Human Review Process

Any content creator or publisher can appeal a flag. Human reviewers — not just the AI — evaluate disputes.

🏠

On-Device Processing

Analysis runs locally on your device when possible, minimizing how much content ever reaches our servers.

Privacy Policy

Your data, your control

What We Collect

When you use [APP NAME], we may collect: (1) anonymized content snippets submitted for analysis, (2) aggregate usage statistics (e.g., how many articles scanned per session), and (3) account information if you create a premium account (email, subscription status). We do not collect full browsing history, personal identifiers linked to specific articles, or any data from content you view but do not submit for analysis.

How We Use It

Anonymized analysis data is used solely to improve model accuracy. Aggregate usage statistics help us understand which features are most useful. We will never sell, license, or share your data with third parties for advertising or profiling purposes.

Your Rights

You may request deletion of any account data at any time. On-device processing means most analysis never leaves your device. You can opt out of anonymous data sharing in settings at any time without losing access to core features.

Data Retention

Anonymized analysis logs are retained for a maximum of 90 days to support model improvement, then permanently deleted. Account information is retained until you request deletion. We do not retain identifiable browsing data under any circumstances.

Research Brief

The Case for [APP NAME]

Anish Velagapudi • Kenan Snider • Baylee Varnell • Gina Byon

Statement of the Problem

Misinformation today rarely takes the form of outright lies — it hides in the architecture of how information is presented. A bar graph with a manipulated baseline, a headline missing critical context, or a statistic cited without its denominator can shape public opinion just as powerfully as fabricated news, yet none of these techniques constitute a factual falsehood that traditional fact-checkers are designed to catch.

According to a 2024 Gallup poll, only 32% of Americans have a "great deal" or "fair amount" of trust in mass media. This erosion of trust suggests that the public senses manipulation but lacks the tools to identify it precisely. The result is a lose-lose: people are either deceived by misleading framing they cannot detect, or they dismiss all media as untrustworthy — an overcorrection that accelerates polarization and makes evidence-based public discourse nearly impossible.

[APP NAME] addresses this gap by giving ordinary users the same analytical tools that trained media critics use — automatically, in real time, and without requiring expertise. This invention is important because the capacity to recognize manipulation is not evenly distributed, and that inequality in media literacy has measurable consequences for how people vote, how they respond to public health guidance, and how they understand their world.

Supporting Research

Finding 1

Online misinformation and deceptive presentation are widespread and growing problems

A comprehensive survey by Security.org (2024) found that the vast majority of Americans report regularly encountering misinformation online, and a significant portion report being unable to identify it when they do. Crucially, the study distinguishes between outright disinformation (deliberately false content) and misinformation — inaccurate or misleading content spread regardless of intent. Misleading presentation of true facts falls squarely in the latter category and is far more common, precisely because it is harder to challenge.

Deceptive data visualizations are a particularly under-studied vector. Research in data journalism and information design has catalogued dozens of chart manipulation techniques — from truncated y-axes to dual-axis graphs that imply false correlations — that routinely appear in mainstream media without any correction or notice. [APP NAME]'s chart analysis module specifically targets this gap.

Finding 2

The market for AI-powered media literacy tools is large, underserved, and commercially viable

According to Statista, there are approximately 331 million internet users in the United States in 2026. Even capturing 1% of that audience as active users — a conservative benchmark for a niche tool — produces a user base of 3.3 million people. At a modest $1 per user per year in ad revenue (industry standard for content-adjacent apps), that floor generates over $3 million annually without a single paid subscriber.

The revenue ceiling is substantially higher. Data from ReachEffect shows that subscription app users generate on average 4.6 times the revenue of ad-only users. A premium tier priced at $5/month — positioned as a civic tool comparable to a news subscription — could push annual revenue to $13–14 million if just 10–15% of active users convert. No direct competitor in the real-time manipulation-detection space currently exists at consumer scale, meaning [APP NAME] has an opportunity to define the category.

Brief Description of the Invention

[APP NAME] is a browser extension and mobile application that uses artificial intelligence to analyze news articles, data visualizations, and video content in real time, flagging patterns of misrepresentation and categorizing them by type. Unlike conventional fact-checkers, which verify factual claims against databases of known falsehoods, [APP NAME] evaluates the structural integrity of how information is presented — detecting manipulated chart baselines, decontextualized statistics, emotionally loaded framing paired with thin evidence, and missing comparative data.

Key features include: real-time scanning with no user input required; a categorized flag system that explains how and why content may be misleading; a chart integrity module using computer vision; video transcript analysis; and a free tier with an optional premium subscription. The system is designed to be privacy-preserving, performing analysis on-device where possible and never storing identifiable browsing data.

Policy Implications

Policymakers should recognize AI-powered media literacy tools as a complement — not a replacement — for platform-level content moderation. Regulatory frameworks should encourage transparency in AI flagging methodologies and mandate bias audits for tools operating at scale. [APP NAME] demonstrates that the market can produce consumer-grade media literacy technology, but government investment in public education programs and potential subsidies for underserved communities could dramatically expand access. Key regulatory challenges include defining "misleading presentation" in a legally coherent way, avoiding chilling effects on legitimate journalism, and ensuring algorithmic accountability.

  • Security.org (2024). "Misinformation and Disinformation Survey."
  • Statista (2026). "Number of internet users in the United States."
  • ReachEffect. "How Much Can an App Make from Advertising?"
